questions.q: Why does this case study identify compliance, security, and recoverability as dominant, while performance and scalability are secondary?
options: Because performance and scalability are never relevant to Financial Services Cloud implementations
Because Financial Services Cloud does not support asynchronous Apex
Because compliance always outranks every other NFR category in every scenario, regardless of business context

Because this firm's data and transaction volumes never approach a scale that forces a difficult performance or scalability trade-off, while regulatory recordkeeping, data confidentiality, and loss scenarios are this business's real risk profile
questions.explain: The modest, steady volume in this scenario means performance and scalability are present but not the forcing function for design decisions here — unlike Lesson 13's retailer, this firm's real risk is driven by regulatory and confidentiality obligations, not volume spikes.

questions.q: Which elicitation technique from Lesson 8 is identified as most productive for this specific scenario, and why?
options: Scenario walkthroughs focused on volume spikes, because this firm's main risk is a holiday traffic surge
Existing SLAs, contracts, and policies — specifically the firm's regulatory obligations and confidentiality commitments, which already exist in writing before the project starts
An NFR checklist, because this is the only technique that applies to regulated industries
Stakeholder interviews with end customers, since advisors have no useful input on NFRs
questions.explain: Because this firm's dominant risk is regulatory and contractual, the most productive elicitation source is the existing written recordkeeping and confidentiality obligations the firm has already accepted, not a volume-focused scenario walkthrough.

questions.q: What should an architect do if a compliance officer's stated regulatory requirement seems internally inconsistent or hard to satisfy with a proposed design?
options: Independently reinterpret the underlying regulation without consulting the compliance officer
Ignore the compliance officer's input and design based on general industry best practice instead

Raise the specific concern back to the compliance officer and get it resolved by the person with the actual regulatory expertise, the same way an ambiguous business requirement would be escalated to its owning stakeholder
Automatically implement the requirement using Salesforce Shield regardless of whether it addresses the concern
questions.explain: Per Lesson 7's framing, the architect's job is to implement a stated compliance requirement faithfully, not to independently interpret the regulation. An apparent inconsistency should be escalated back to the compliance stakeholder who owns the requirement.

questions.q: Why is Salesforce Shield's Event Monitoring easy to justify in this scenario specifically?
options: Because the compliance officer's stated requirement — detecting and proving who accessed which client's data, and when — is exactly the capability Event Monitoring is built to provide
Because Event Monitoring is required by law for every Salesforce org handling financial data
Because Event Monitoring eliminates the need for field-level security on account balance fields
Because Event Monitoring is free for all Financial Services Cloud customers
questions.explain: Recommending Shield should be driven by a specific NFR the base platform doesn't already satisfy (Lesson 3) — here, the compliance officer's explicit access-logging and audit requirement maps directly onto what Event Monitoring is designed to do.

questions.q: What does the "lost or stolen advisor laptop" scenario in this case study actually test, according to the lesson?
options: Whether the firm's device-replacement budget is adequate
Whether the firm's Service Cloud implementation meets its performance NFR
Whether the Salesforce mobile app can run offline

Whether the firm's data-loss-prevention posture and backup/audit trail can prove what was and wasn't exposed, and whether client records remain intact and recoverable regardless of what happened to any one device
questions.explain: The scenario isn't really about the device itself — it's a test of recoverability and data-loss-prevention: can the firm prove what was exposed, and are the actual client records still safe and recoverable independent of what happened to that one laptop.
